column5: shepherd leads in paths of righteousness
column6: The shepherd restores the traveler and leads him in righteous tracks, a direct shepherd-guide form of the requested path.

column5: rod and staff in the dark valley
column6: The commentary's staff goes ahead as a guide; in this walking-through-danger scene the shepherd's rod and staff comfort the traveler, giving the object a related but not identical role.

column5: dwelling in the LORD's house
column6: The psalm's guided traveler ends by dwelling in the LORD's house, supplying the homeward terminus paired with the commentary's route.

column5: righteousness goes before and makes a way
column6: Righteousness goes before God and makes a way from his steps, a poetic image of a preceding presence whose passage establishes the route.

column5: good Spirit leads on level ground
column6: The prayer asks for the good Spirit to lead the speaker on level ground, directly combining divine guidance with the commentary's flat, passable road.

column5: snares laid beside a path
column6: The enemies spread nets and snares beside the path, a close physical counterpart to the hostile figure waiting upon and around the straight way.

column5: make me walk in the path of commandments
column6: The psalmist asks to be made to walk in the path of commandments because he delights in it, preserving both a prayer for guidance and ongoing habitual movement.

column5: teach the way to walk and the deed to do
column6: Moses is to make known the way people must walk and the work they must do, joining instruction, route, and daily practice as the commentary does.

column5: show us the way to walk and what to do
column6: The remnant asks God to show the particular way it should walk and the act it should perform, a communal prayer that closely parallels ihdinā.

column5: shepherd seeks scattered sheep on a dark day
column6: God promises to seek his flock amid its scattering, extending the earlier lost-sheep scene into the restoring action of a true guide.

column5: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
column6: The divine shepherd seeks the lost and brings back the strayed, directly answering the commentary's lost traveler and the companions who call him toward guidance.

column5: the LORD before and Israel's God behind
column6: The return is protected by a God who goes before and also guards from behind, an illuminating reversal of the commentary's vulnerable traveler surrounded by threats.

column5: priest walks in peace and uprightness, turns many
column6: The exemplary priest walks with God in peace and uprightness and turns many from iniquity, joining straight conduct with a guide's effect on others.

column5: teachers cause many to stumble by instruction
column6: The corrupt priests cause many to stumble through their teaching, a precise institutional inverse to the knowledgeable guide who keeps followers from losing the way.

column5: highway joining nations in shared worship
column6: A highway enables movement between Egypt and Assyria and culminates in shared worship; it gives the commentary's communal worship-road an international, reconciliatory form.

column5: Wisdom guides by way, shelter by day, stars by night
column6: Wisdom guides the holy people along a remarkable way and becomes their shelter by day and starlight by night, unusually gathering guide, road, and celestial orientation signs.

column5: walking God's way and lasting peace
column6: Baruch says that walking God's way would have meant living in peace forever, a concise route-to-destination formulation.

column5: God leads Israel with joy in light
column6: Following its road-leveling scene, Baruch says God will lead Israel with joy in the light of divine glory, adding visible guidance to the returning community.

column5: narrow city-road bordered by fire and water
column6: The angel's image of the one narrow entrance to a city, with fire on one side and deep water on the other, makes remaining on a central course a matter of reaching one's home.

column5: traveler consults the Creator before setting out
column6: The talmud identifies consulting God before a journey with the traveler's prayer, giving a rabbinic liturgical practice for seeking protection and direction on a road.

column5: following the light avoids darkness
column6: Jesus says that the one following him will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life, directly linking leader, walking, light, and non-lost arrival.

column5: walker in darkness does not know the destination
column6: The warning to walk while light is present says darkness overtakes the person who walks without knowing where he goes, a close counterpart to the commentary's disoriented traveler.

column5: serving Jesus, following him, being where he is
column6: The commentary's cited Jesus directs worship to God as the straight path; John joins serving Jesus to following him and being where he is, so the object of service and path-following differs materially.

column5: Spirit of truth guides into all truth
column6: The Spirit is promised as a guide into all truth; the guidance is interpretive rather than a road scene, but it preserves the commentary's leading rather than mere information.

column5: angel directs Philip onto the Gaza road
column6: An angel sends Philip onto a specific desert road, making divine guidance an actual route instruction before the encounter with the traveler.

column5: unless someone guides me
column6: On the road, the Ethiopian says he cannot understand unless someone guides him, a direct verbal and scene-level counterpart to needing a guide for the way.

column5: instructed in the way of the Lord
column6: Apollos is instructed in the way of the Lord and teaches concerning Jesus, giving the Way an explicit pedagogical form alongside the commentary's guide who makes a path known.

column5: blind man gains sight and follows on the way
column6: The healed blind man immediately follows Jesus on the way, bringing sight, recovery from disorientation, and following a leader into one movement.

column5: self-styled guide of the blind and light in darkness
column6: Paul reports the claim to be a guide of blind people and a light in darkness in a critical context; it provides a qualified counterexample to the authority of a guide.

column5: those led by God's Spirit are God's children
column6: The verse makes being led by God's Spirit a defining relation of God's children, an abstract but specific counterpart to a community guided by God.

column5: good works prepared beforehand to walk in
column6: God prepares good works beforehand so that believers may walk in them, making a divinely prepared course the form of sustained practice.

column5: walk worthy toward God's kingdom and glory
column6: Paul urges conduct worthy of the God who calls believers into kingdom and glory, joining a moral walk to a destination beyond the journey.

column5: way into the sanctuary not yet manifest
column6: The Spirit indicates that the way into the holy place was not yet open, supplying the inaccessible-side context for the later new and living way.

column5: heavenly homeland and a prepared city
column6: The pilgrims seek a better, heavenly homeland and God prepares a city for them, a destination image that complements the commentary's road-and-house pairing.

column5: no lasting city here, seeking the coming one
column6: The community has no permanent city here and seeks the coming city, turning road imagery into an ongoing search for a final dwelling.

column5: nations walk by the city's light
column6: The nations walk by the New Jerusalem's light, an eschatological convergence of collective travel, orienting light, and the city as destination.
